summary: Specifies a set of solutions for the replication and distributed operation problems raised when building an Internet Directory using X.500 (1988). It was on the standards track and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1276 describes an interim way to replicate X.500 directory data and route queries when servers cannot all communicate directly. The RFC warns that the approach has limits in manageability and scalability, and the unit metadata marks it Historic.

subtitle: An interim approach to X.500 directory replication and distributed lookups.

tldr.problem: An Internet directory based on X.500 needed replication and query handling across networks without universal direct connectivity. Stable standards for these requirements were not yet available.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents an interim approach based on the QUIPU implementation: it replicates groups of sibling entries called Entry Data Blocks and defines how directory servers can relay queries across communities.
tldr.outcome: The RFC calls its approach interim and notes known limits in management and scaling. The unit metadata classifies it as Historic and lists no replacement RFC.

today: RFC 1276 is Historic according to the unit metadata, which lists no replacement RFC. The RFC itself describes the procedures as interim and says they have known limits in manageability and scalability.

sections.title: Why the RFC Defines an Interim Approach
sections.content:
The RFC says that Internet directory requirements described in RFC 1275 did not yet have stable standards-based solutions. Waiting for those standards could delay a useful pilot, so the document records a simpler approach already used in the QUIPU implementation.

The authors explicitly describe the procedures as interim. They note known manageability and scalability deficiencies and expect transition to standard approaches when appropriate standards become available.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors documented an approach that was already in use while standards work continued. They state that it is temporary and has known limits.

sections.title: Queries Across Network Communities
sections.content:
The RFC defines a community as a network environment in which entities can communicate directly. A directory server can pass a referral only when it believes the caller can reach the referred server. If the caller and referred server cannot communicate directly, the query can be sent through a server higher in the directory tree or through a relay server that belongs to both communities.

The procedures are requirements for conforming directory servers. The document does not place requirements on user agents. It also allows a referral to list a master and slave copy, with the master first.
sections.plainLanguage: A server should refer a query only to a server the caller can reach. If they cannot communicate directly, another directory server can pass the query across the network boundary.

sections.title: Entry Data Blocks
sections.content:
The replication unit is an Entry Data Block (EDB): the complete set of immediate child entries under a parent entry. It includes each child's relative name, attributes, and knowledge information. A server that holds non-cached information for an entry also holds information about all of its siblings.

One server holds the master EDB, and other servers can hold slave copies. The RFC says that this arrangement can simplify name resolution and improve single-level searching and listing compared with a more general approach that might contact many servers.
sections.plainLanguage: An EDB contains all immediate child entries under one directory entry. Servers can copy the block so they have a local copy of that part of the directory.

sections.title: Pulling and Updating a Directory Copy
sections.content:
The GetEntryDataBlock operation lets one server request an EDB from another. Normally the requester supplies the version it holds, and the server returns the EDB if its copy is newer. The requester can ask only for a version number or force a complete retrieval.

Large EDBs can be transferred in chunks by limiting the number of entries in each response and using the returned next-entry position to continue. The RFC notes that this whole-block method is simpler but less efficient than incremental replication. It also discusses how updates can be handled while a transfer is in progress.
sections.plainLanguage: A server asks for an EDB version and receives a newer copy when one is available. Large copies can be split into chunks, but the method transfers whole blocks rather than individual changes.

sections.title: Scaling and Security Limits
sections.content:
The RFC identifies non-incremental updates as the main scaling limit. Given the assumptions stated in the document about entry size and transfer size, it estimates a fanout limit of about 10,000 and says the method is intended for high levels of the directory tree. Other replication methods are not excluded.

Applications may use replicated data for ordinary reads. If they suspect that a copy is stale, they can repeat the request while prohibiting use of copy data. The RFC says that security considerations are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: Copying a complete block limits how large a directory branch can be for this approach. The RFC says it is intended for higher levels of the directory, and it does not discuss security.
